 Pete Rose, Barry Bonds and Roger Clemens all deserve to be in the Baseball Hall of Fame
 By
 Ryan Canfield Fox News 
 Published

 close Video Trump grants posthumous pardon to baseball legend Pete Rose 
 President Donald Trump announces a posthumous pardon for Pete Rose over his 1990 federal tax convictions, while criticizing Major League Baseball’s treatment of its career hits leader. Chad Pergram reports on the decision and Rose’s legacy, including his 1989 gambling ban and posthumous reinstatement in 2025.
 OPINION: Major League Baseball's hit king, home run king and the pitcher who has won the most Cy Young Awards in the history of the sport are not in the Baseball Hall of Fame.
 Doesn't something seem wrong with that picture? In every sport, the top players are either in their respective halls of fame or will be voted in soon. Yet in baseball, that isn't the case.
 With President Donald Trump's "full and complete" posthumous pardon of Pete Rose, it feels like a good time to bring up the fact that he, Barry Bonds and Roger Clemens should all be in Cooperstown.

 Cincinnati Reds Hall of Famer Pete Rose adjusts his cap as he takes the microphone during a pregame ceremony for the unveiling of his bronze statue outside Great American Ball Park in Cincinnati, Ohio, before the MLB National League game between the Cincinnati Reds and the Los Angeles Dodgers on Saturday, June 17, 2017. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect) 
 Rose, who died in 2024 at age 83 , was banned from baseball in 1989 over gambling allegations, and admitted to betting on baseball in 2004. He later served five months in prison after pleading guilty to federal tax charges.
 Rose would undoubtedly be in the Baseball Hall of Fame if his statistics on the field outweighed his violation of the sport's golden rule. Rose is MLB’s hit king, with 4,256 career hits. He was the National League MVP in 1973, a 17-time All-Star, a three-time World Series champion and a three-time batting title winner.
 While he broke the golden rule, there are no official findings that Rose ever bet against himself or his own team. What Rose did was not like what former Cleveland Guardians closer Emmanuel Clase is accused of doing: throwing suspicious pitches to aid bettors. Clase allegedly deliberately altered his pitch speeds and outcomes to help bettors.
 Clase allegedly performed worse intentionally to aid bettors. Rose never bet against his own team. The two situations are completely different.
 Now, did Rose's decision to bet on his team as a manager affect the team? It absolutely could have.
 For example, if Rose bet on the Cincinnati Reds to win on a Tuesday, would he push a reliever who had pitched the previous two days to pitch for a third consecutive day in a game in which he otherwise might not have used him if he hadn't gambled?

 Cincinnati Reds manager Pete Rose stands with coaches Tommy Helms and Scott Breeden on April 9, 1989. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect) 
 If he deployed that relief pitcher simply because he wanted his best option on the mound to win his bet, the Reds might be worse off on Wednesday. That same reliever might be needed Wednesday, but because Rose used him in a game he bet on, the pitcher might not be available.
 Rose's shortsighted bullpen management due to his gambling could have hurt the Reds in the long term.
 It wasn't until after Rose's death that he was removed from MLB's permanently ineligible list on May 13, 2025. While he has been removed from the list, that doesn't guarantee his induction into the Baseball Hall of Fame because of how the committee may view his gambling, even though he only bet on his own team.
 Rose's first opportunity to be voted into the Baseball Hall of Fame will come in December 2027, when the Classic Baseball Era Committee considers candidates for induction.
 And I think they should vote him in. I understand how difficult it may be to vote someone in who broke the sport's golden rule.
 But how seriously does Major League Baseball take gambling anymore? MLB partnered with FanDuel, a major sportsbook, in 2023. You cannot watch a baseball game without seeing multiple gambling ads or attend a baseball game without seeing multiple gambling advertisements plastered throughout the stadium.
 Gambling promotion is ubiquitous throughout baseball. Now, just because MLB promotes gambling incessantly doesn't mean that players and managers should all start betting on themselves.

 San Francisco Giants legend Barry Bonds is introduced before the game against the Seattle Mariners at Oracle Park in San Francisco, Calif., on April 4, 2025. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect) 
 But, with that being said, I still think Rose deserves to be in Cooperstown. The player who has the most hits in Major League Baseball history deserves to be in the Baseball Hall of Fame. If he bet against his team, I'd take the opposite position and be pounding on the table against his inclusion.
 But that said, I still think Rose deserves to be in Cooperstown. The player who has the most hits in Major League Baseball history deserves to be in the Baseball Hall of Fame. If he had bet against his team, I'd take the opposite position and pound on the table against his inclusion.
 The Baseball Hall of Fame respectfully declined to comment on Trump's pardon of Rose .
 Now, as for Bonds and Clemens , their presumed steroid use is why they aren't in the Hall of Fame. Clemens has consistently denied using steroids, while Bonds has maintained that he didn't knowingly take any steroids.
 Regardless of whether they used steroids, they should both be in Cooperstown.
 Why? Major League Baseball didn't implement performance-enhancing drug (PED) testing until 2003.
 The sport's popularity took a massive hit after the 1994-95 players' strike . The home run races in the late 1990s helped revive baseball and return it to cultural relevance.
 LONGTIME SPORTS BROADCASTER BOB COSTAS CALLS DONALD TRUMP A 'SOCIOPATH' IN WILD RANT 
 Barry Bonds addresses the crowd during his induction into the Pittsburgh Pirates Hall of Fame at PNC Park in Pittsburgh, Pa., on Aug. 24, 2024. (USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con) 
 If you weren't going to punish Bonds, whose 762 home runs, 2,558 walks, 688 intentional walks and 162.8 bWAR are all MLB records, and who was a seven-time MVP and 14-time All-Star during a career that spanned 1986 to 2007, then why punish him now?
 If you weren't going to punish Clemens, a seven-time Cy Young Award winner, two-time World Series champion, 11-time All-Star and 1986 American League MVP, during his career from 1984 to 2007 , then why punish him now?
 You cannot tell the story of baseball without talking about Bonds and Clemens. You simply cannot.
 Setting their presumed steroid use aside, I do not think it's fair to exclude Bonds and Clemens from the Baseball Hall of Fame when Major League Baseball didn't test for performance-enhancing drugs until the tail end of their careers.
 If it wasn't something they could have been punished for during the majority of their playing days, they shouldn't be punished now.
 There are some people within the Baseball Writers' Association of America who agree. Bonds received 66% of the vote in his final year on the ballot, short of the 75% required to earn induction.
 Former New York Yankees pitcher Roger Clemens attends the Old Timer's Day Ceremony at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx, N.Y., on Aug. 9, 2025. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

 Clemens peaked at 65.2% in his final year on the ballot. Unfortunately for him, he isn't eligible to be voted in again until 2031 because he received fewer than five votes from the 16-member Contemporary Baseball Era Committee in December 2025. As a result, he became ineligible for the next three-year cycle under Hall of Fame rules. Bonds, who also received fewer than five votes from the committee, isn't eligible until 2031, either.
 Rose has more hits than anyone in MLB history. Bonds has more home runs than anyone in MLB history. Clemens has more Cy Young Awards than any pitcher in MLB history.
 It's time for the Baseball Hall of Fame to recognize all three.
